canberra.title: Landmark lyric theatre rises from the ground
canberra.snippet: It’s been a hole in the ground for months but now one of the most significant developments in Canberra’s artistic history is ...
canberra.content:
Canberra Lyric Theatre development. Photos: John Lomnicki and ACT Government.

It’s been a hole in the ground for months but now one of the most significant developments in Canberra’s artistic history is heading skywards to become a fixture in the CBD landscape and a reality in Canberrans’ minds.

The new four-level, 2000-seat lyric theatre which will revolutionise the national capital’s performance and cultural experience is rising out of the excavations and providing onlookers with a glimpse of what is to come.

Photos of the site reveal the stage and orchestra pit taking shape, and Infrastructure Canberra has released new renders and fly-through video of the theatre.

Since construction commenced in January, tier 1 builder Multiplex has completed the installation of deep foundation piles, excavation of basement areas and significant structural concrete works.

The deepest excavation point on the site – the orchestra pit – is also complete, and essential services are being installed, including stormwater systems, sewer infrastructure, lift shafts and other utility connections that will support the safe and efficient operation of the theatre.

With foundation works approaching completion, construction has now progressed to the theatre’s stage and floor, which will be followed by installation of the roof and facade, giving the theatre its distinctive architectural identity.

Infrastructure Canberra Program Director, Arts and Sports Infrastructure, Julia Pucci said it was a significant milestone for the project, which will be an architectural landmark for such a key corner in the city and enable big touring shows which previously would not consider Canberra to now stage their productions here.

“You can start to see the orchestra pit forming, and we’ve got the first bit of vertical structure coming up with the fire stairs and lift structure, which will be repeated on the other side of the orchestra pit as well,” she said.

Ms Pucci said it was a complex build but Multiplex had plenty of experience in such projects.

It was now all about planning and execution, with a lot of big structural elements, big pieces of steel, that would be arriving.

Canberrans would see the building levels take shape quite rapidly as it emerges from the foundations, followed by the facade towards the end of the year or early next year.

In the first quarter of 2027 the roof would go on to “get watertight” and then the internal fitout would begin.

“It’s very complicated for a theatre; the whole thing’s like a finely tuned instrument,” Ms Pucci said.

A key part of the building was the triangular skylight. The notion of sky country was one of the design principles that came about through designing with country and consulting with local Indigenous families.

“In the daytime you’ll look up and see the sky, and in the evening you look up and see the stars. That connection to the sky is a really important part of the architectural design, and it’s lovely because it lets the light in as well,” Ms Pucci said.

The materials and colours seen in the design have been inspired by the Canberra region, including the woodlands of Black Mountain, the granite of Birrigai and Namadgi, the ochres of Mount Ainslie, and the textures of the Molonglo River corridor.

Ms Pucci said it would be an impressive building and an amazing place to see a show.

“The theatre’s going to be just beautiful, so I think people will be really proud of it,” she said.

“It’s very thoughtful for the back of house as well, so I think performers will really enjoy being there.”

Ms Pucci said the project was on track, on time and on budget.

It was expected to be completed by mid-2028 and then it was up to the Cultural Facilities Corporation that runs the Canberra Theatre Centre to decide when the new theatre would be ready for its first opening night.

Canberra Theatre Centre Executive Director Georgia Hendy said it was an exciting time for Canberra as the city moved closer to welcoming a venue unlike anything it had seen before.

“With greater capacity and contemporary facilities, this new venue will enable us to attract major productions, strengthening the city’s place on the national touring circuit while delivering an exceptional experience for audiences from the moment they walk through the doors,” she said.

“The new lyric theatre will allow Canberra Theatre Centre to further enrich our city’s cultural life, support the continued growth of our local creative sector and ensure future generations can continue to experience unforgettable live performances right here in our Nation’s Capital.”

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the design and progress of construction showed the scale and ambition of this project.

As well as attracting major productions that currently bypass Canberra, the lyric theatre by year five of operation was projected to contribute almost $34 million each year to Canberra’s economy and generate more than 111,000 visitor nights a year.

“The venue will attract new visitors, support local restaurants, cafes, hotels and businesses, and create jobs across the arts, events and hospitality sectors,” Mr Barr said.

“The new theatre, along with other major projects such as the National Convention and Entertainment Centre, is central to our vision for a connected and thriving city centre.

“Together, these once-in-a-generation projects are part of our plan for Canberra – helping to reshape our city centre, support jobs and economic growth, and create new reasons for people to spend time in the city.”

The progress of the project can be followed on the BuiltforCBR website.

canberra.title: The Canberra Bookshelf: Girls both bad and good
canberra.snippet: The Followers (Maree Spratt, Allen & Unwin, Australia, 2026, cover design Christa Moffat, Christabella Designs, cover illustrations N...
canberra.content:
The Followers is a tale of girlhood bullying and redemption. Image: Supplied.

The Followers (Maree Spratt, Allen & Unwin, Australia, 2026, cover design Christa Moffat, Christabella Designs, cover illustrations Nastia/Adobe Stock) is a whip-smart fiction, delving into the dark hothouse that girlhood can be from pre-puberty, through teenhood and into young womanhood.

There was a time when we could easily leave our girlhoods behind if we chose to, but contemporary life provides the ever-present temptation of social media and its ability to peer into the lives of people with whom we grew up.

Told mostly in the voice of Teresa, the story follows her ache to be one of the “in crowd” – a desire which encourages, nay demands, the surrender of a moral compass.

Queen Bee of the in crowd in Teresa’s life is Lacey, whose power to command obedience in her acolytes seems endless. Nevertheless, this wealthy child leads a rudderless life of parental neglect, finding her philosophy through popular glossy magazines.

The school playground populace is held thrall via the weapon of the marble competition. Lacey’s group rules the roost, determining who can play and who cannot.

Into the mix comes the socially disadvantaged Carmel Strongman, who becomes the whipping boy for the elite group, is treated abominably and then disappears from their lives. She is soon a thorn in Lacey’s side via her outstanding skill at marbles.

It is probably not too much of a giveaway to reveal that the abominable bullying of Carmel is not the last word and that in her way Carmel steals that from the later life Lacey, who has, also not surprisingly, become a hugely popular wellness and lifestyle Influencer.

The author has deftly managed to subtly direct the reader’s attention to the diverse parenting styles and models of family we expect to see in contemporary society. How well children survive their early years is equally as diverse and not dependent upon wealth, but upon love.

Whilst we are deep in the mind of Teresa for much of the story, the book invites us to question the reliability of this prime witness, who even in adulthood seems to be skewing her memories in order to not look so bad – such a human thing to do, it must be said.

In her examination of human nature, Maree Spratt proves herself to be an astute and curious observer. She sometimes makes us cringe; at other times we recoil in horror at the darkness of the human soul. We equally fist pump the small victories. It’s a clever and complex piece of writing but also always entertaining.

Pocket-loving Poppy reminds us of the value of small treasures and of helping friends. Image: Supplied.

A gentler view of girlhood is to be found in Jemima Parker and Karen Erasmus’ Poppy makes pockets (EK Books, Australia, 2026, (Book design Mark Thacker).

Jemima Parker’s charming story of a creative and resourceful little girl reminds us of the importance of following through one’s ideas, of valuing small treasures and of helping one’s friends.

Poppy is determined to have garments with pockets so that she can collect natural treasures when she’s out walking in nature – after all, who doesn’t love a garment with pockets so there is somewhere to put one’s things!

With laudable economy and the help of her family, she repurposes old T-shirts to make pockets, which she decorates with hand stitching. She then goes a step further and offers then freely to all comers at her roadside stall.

By incorporating a stream of friends from diverse cultures, the author gets another message into the story whilst also pointing to the wide range of interests our friends can have.

It’s a story with clear but not preachy messages of inclusivity and creativity, co-operation and gratitude, of the fulfilment we feel when we do something worthwhile that can both satisfy our own needs and help others.

The book also includes instructions for readers to make their own pockets.

Karen Erasmus has created the perfect visual story alongside the words. Her pictures are expressive of the personalities of the characters and full of interesting details that children will love. This is a joyous book.

canberra.title: When is it bullying and when is it friendship conflict? Canberra parents face a growing dilemma
canberra.snippet: Scroll through the Canberra Community groups on almost any day, and one concern surfaces again and again: bullying in schools. Parents de...
canberra.content:
Parents should resist the temptation to immediately label every difficult friendship as bullying. Photo: Mark Piovesan.

Scroll through the Canberra Community groups on almost any day, and one concern surfaces again and again: bullying in schools.

Parents describe children refusing to go to school, friendship groups breaking down, cruel comments about appearance and social exclusion. Some ask whether they should change schools. Others wonder if homeschooling is the only answer.

There is little doubt bullying exists. Canberra has seen several serious cases in recent months, and schools, parents and policymakers continue to grapple with how to respond.

But as more parents seek help online, psychologists say another conversation is becoming just as important – understanding when a child is being bullied and when they are experiencing the difficult, but often normal, conflicts that come with growing up.

One Canberra mother recently shared her fears after watching her daughter’s friendship group unravel over several months.

She described repeated exclusion, pressure to reveal secrets, rumours, criticism of other children’s appearance and being left out of birthday parties. Her daughter has now reached the point where she no longer wants to go to school.

Another parent sought advice after her seven-year-old daughter was repeatedly called both “fat” and “too skinny” by classmates. She said the comments had begun affecting her daughter’s eating habits, with the child sometimes refusing food despite being hungry.

Nesh Nikolic, managing director and principal clinical psychologist at Strategic Psychology, says parents should resist the temptation to immediately label every difficult friendship as bullying.

“Friendship conflict is usually reciprocal, time-limited and occurs within a relationship that still has moments of connection or repair,” he said.

“Children argue, exclude or say unkind things. While hurtful, these behaviours often form part of learning social boundaries.”

Bullying, he says, looks different. It is usually repeated, involves an imbalance of power and continues despite the child’s distress. Over time, it begins affecting daily life, whether through anxiety, withdrawal or refusing to attend school.

Rather than focusing on a single incident, he encourages parents to look for patterns.

“The same behaviour – exclusion, rumours or a dirty look – can sit on a continuum depending on how often it happens, the wider context and the impact it has on the child.”

Nikolic believes greater awareness of bullying has been overwhelmingly positive, but says it has also changed the way parents interpret children’s social experiences.

“There is a risk that parents and schools sometimes move quickly to the ‘bullying’ label,” he said.

While that vigilance helps protect children experiencing genuine harm, he warns it can also leave children with fewer opportunities to learn how to repair friendships, resolve disagreements and navigate relationships that are sometimes messy.

That doesn’t mean parents should dismiss what their child is feeling.

Instead, he encourages them to listen carefully, validate their child’s experience and help them think through possible responses before immediately stepping in to solve the problem.

Children benefit from learning how to communicate boundaries, seek support from trusted adults and build friendships beyond one difficult relationship, he said.

Looking at the first Canberra case, Nikolic said the length of time the behaviour had continued, together with the child’s reluctance to attend school, suggested more than an ordinary disagreement.

At the same time, because the girls had known each other since daycare and the families had a long relationship, he believes the situation should be approached as a complex friendship problem rather than simply identifying one child as the bully and the other as the victim.

He encourages parents to work collaboratively with schools and, where appropriate, other families, focusing on helping all children develop empathy, inclusion and conflict-resolution skills.

Professional support should also be considered if parents notice sustained changes in a child’s mood, sleep, appetite or willingness to attend school.

Ultimately, Nikolic says the goal should extend beyond stopping bullying.

“Children need adults who can hold the complexity of peer relationships,” he said.

“They need protection from genuine harm while still being trusted to practise the difficult, imperfect skills of repair, resilience and mutual consideration.”

For parents navigating playground politics, that balance may be one of the hardest parts of raising children.

Protecting them when they need it.

But also giving them the confidence to discover they are capable of working through conflict when they can.

canberra.title: Northbourne’s contemporary Japanese dining that won’t leave you out in the cold
canberra.snippet: It’s hard to keep a good Canberran down, and there isn’t a true and loyal Canberran who, at some point in their life, hasn’t gone into ba...
canberra.content:
Don’t let the judgemental squid turn you off the raw seafood menu. Photo: Tenele Conway.

It’s hard to keep a good Canberran down, and there isn’t a true and loyal Canberran who, at some point in their life, hasn’t gone into battle to defend the credibility of our nightlife.

But walking down Northbourne Avenue, a stone’s throw from the London Circuit closure on an arctic Monday night, it’s easy to question where your loyalty really lies. The vibe is decidedly post-apocalyptic.

It’s a scene that every hardy Canberran knows only too well, but against all odds, life is out there, and Northbourne’s contemporary Japanese restaurant Chop Chop is one such place offering good times, great food and a solid commitment to paying their heating bill.

Birthed from its former incarnation, Edo Tori, Chop Chop came onto the scene in 2023, and if you haven’t yet been, it’s worth a London Circuit detour.

The Wagyu beef skewers with edamame and Asahi on tap are a strong combo. Photo: Martin Conway.

Filled with neon fun, bold and eclectic murals and a price point that won’t make you clutch your heart, Chop Chop is easy to love, even when Canberra is doing its best to break you.

When it comes to ordering, the laziest among us can opt for a Feed Me menu priced at $69 per person. It’s jumped up a little in price since my last visit. However, what hasn’t changed is that it’s still excellent value, given that you’ll receive a procession of nine dishes, including several types of sashimi and a well-balanced mix of sharing dishes, all leaning into Chop Chop’s unique blend of tradition and innovation.

Already familiar with the Feed Me menu, we weighed up the wider selection on offer, with the salmon carpaccio hitting the table first. Reaching in with my chopsticks and mopping the salmon through its fruity, smoky sauce, I was aware of the oversized mural squid sitting in judgement behind us; little did he know, I reckoned with my carnivorous ways long ago and not even his cute orange face was going to stop me getting my fill.

The salmon carpaccio is sweet, smoky and delicious. Photo: Martin Conway.

We paired the salmon with some edamame topped with big dollops of sesame-infused sauce. This was chased down with the wagyu beef skewers that were nicely charred, perfectly tender and smothered in a sweet, smoky soy-based sauce.

From our selection of small plates, it was agreed that the negi hotate scallops, served on the shell with micro herbs and crisp onion, were the standout so far, although one more dish was still to arrive.

The negi hotate scallops were the standout among our small plates. Photo: Martin Conway.

Waiting for the final dish and sipping on our Asahi poured from the selection of eight beers on tap, the poignant neon signage above the bar catches my eye: ‘Save Water Drink Beer’. It’s a message that really resonates with me at this stage of life; it’s a more mature take on the old mantra, ‘Live Laugh Love’.

Searching Temu for a homewares edition for my mantlepiece, our final main arrives: the Tori chicken breast.

Consisting of a grilled and sliced chicken breast with a herb yoghurt and cabbage pickle, it wrapped up what was not only a reasonably priced meal, but one that I can enter into My Fitness Pal without having to lie to retain my stats (let’s keep the beer between you and me, though).

The Tori chicken breast wrapped up a delicious and reasonably-priced meal. Photo: Martin Conway.

Stepping back out onto the blustery main road and saying sayonara to the warm haven of Chop Chop, it’s nice to reflect on the fact that our great city has never struggled to produce good food, only to persuade people to leave the house to find it.

Chop Chop is located at 43 Northbourne Ave, Canberra. They’re open from 5:30 pm until 9 pm, Monday through Wednesday, and from 12 pm until 2:30 pm and 5:30 pm until 9:30 pm Thursday through Sunday.

canberra.title: How a getaway in Sydney saved Tidbinbilla platypuses from drought
canberra.snippet: When several platypuses took a holiday at Taronga Zoo in Sydney, it was just the start of a journey that has shed light on conservation w...
canberra.content:
Seven platypuses were rescued from Tidbinbilla during a severe drought. Photos: Taronga Conservation Society Australia.

When several platypuses took a holiday at Taronga Zoo in Sydney, it was just the start of a journey that has shed light on conservation work for their species as a whole.

Seven platypuses (two males and five females) were rescued from the drought-stricken Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve in December 2019.

The interconnected pond system within the reserve dropped to critically low levels during the 2017-19 drought, likely resulting in the deaths of multiple platypuses by mid-2019.

Researchers from Taronga Conservation Society Australia and UNSW Sydney’s Centre for Ecosystem Science teamed up with officers from ACT Parks and Conservation for the evacuation.

Ultimately, five platypuses were returned to Tidbinbilla after a five-month stay at Taronga Zoo (one male escaped after arrival, while another died after becoming trapped in part of its enclosure).

They had been surgically fitted with acoustic transmitters, which the researchers used to track their movements for 18 months.

Their findings were published this month.

“Tidbinbilla, in a sense, is an interesting case – it’s where the reserve itself offers really good habitat when conditions are favourable,” lead author and University of NSW Associate Professor Gilad Bino says.

“But as waterways dry up there … [the platypuses are], in a sense, stranded there.”

Associate Professor Bino says the tracking devices meant they could keep a close eye on the mammals when the five survivors were returned to Tidbinbilla in May 2020.

“[Those transmitters] really gave us the ability to track these platypuses over really extensive periods of time, and conclude that they were establishing well and returned to kind of their normal habits, settling into kind of their areas.”

One of the repatriated platypuses wasn’t detected after 39 days, though their fate remains unknown as no body was recovered.

According to their study, it’s believed to be the first to quantify the post-release movements of returned platypuses after a drought-driven evacuation.

The four female platypuses exhibited consistent site preferences, whereas the male visited more sites throughout the area covered by the transmitters.

But all went to their capture locations and showed typical foraging behaviour within days of being released back into Tidbinbilla.

He says continued monitoring has revealed there are currently about 20 platypuses in the reserve.

One of the rescued platypuses receiving a check-up upon arrival at Taronga Zoo. Photos: Taronga Conservation Society Australia.

But Associate Professor Bino warns that more animals could face similar problems as their habitats are continually fragmented and affected by climate change.

He says that these platypuses settled back into life at Tidbinbilla quickly, raising hopes others could be evacuated if their habitat hits a crisis point.

“The next drought will hit us, without a doubt, at some point. Really, habitat restoration is the best strategy, the most cost-effective strategy … and restoration can only happen with communities.

“It’s not enough for us to rely on protected areas to safeguard platypuses.”

He says their results shine a light on the undeniable impact humans are having on the environment.

“We have to remember that we’re in this space now of undertaking intensive conservation actions because of the impact that we’ve had on our environment in terms of destroying habitat, fragmenting populations,” he says.

“We have to, in a sense, jump into this natural process and assume this role of facilitating connectivity, of movement of individuals to safe havens or to temporary facilities.

“Ideally, we wouldn’t have to be here if we would take care of our environment.”

australia.title: Victorian Labor promises free dental care if re-elected in Australia-first move
australia.snippet: Premier Ben Carroll says $230m would be earmarked for 10 public dental clinics to operate on a walk-in basis Get our breaking news email ...
australia.content:
Victorians would be able to walk into a dental clinic and receive free checkups and treatment under an Australian-first proposal the Labor government will take to the November state election.

The premier, Ben Carroll, will announce the plan – Labor’s first major election commitment – at a rally on Saturday to mark fewer than 100 days until Victorians go to the polls.

Carroll will say a re-elected Labor government would spend $230m to open 10 public dental clinics across the state, where oral care clinicians would be able to provide free checkups and treatments, including fillings, root canals and extractions.

Carroll described the plan as “structural cost-of-living support” and a national-first intervention by a state government.

“Only Labor will deliver free dental care for all Victorians,” he said in a statement.

On Saturday, Caroll told reporters the government was aiming to have the 10 clinics open by the middle of 2027.

The health minister, Ingrid Stitt, has described the plan as the dental equivalent of the state’s urgent care clinics, where people can “turn up and get the care you need”.

“Getting dental care shouldn’t be determined by your bank balance or where you live,” Stitt said.

Following the announcement, an opposition spokesperson said the government’s “mismanagement of our health system” meant the median waiting time for public dental care in Victoria was seven months, compared to one month in NSW, according to Productivity Commission data.

“Labor can’t staff the dental services we already have, yet want Victorians to believe they can suddenly provide free dental care for seven million people,” they said.

Asked about high vacancy rates among dentists on Saturday, Stitt told reporters the government would have more to about “the workforce component of this election commitment”.

The Victorian Greens said the announcement of a “handful of free dental clinics shows that Labor only acts on the cost of living when it faces electoral wipeout”.

“It’s a start – but with only enough places for a stadium’s worth of Victorians, getting an appointment will be harder than scoring Taylor Swift tickets,” said health spokesperson, Dr Sarah Mansfield.

The Victorian Council of Social Service (Vcoss) welcomed the announcement, but called on the government to ensure “that these services are designed to reach low-income Victorians first and foremost”.

Vcoss CEO Juanita Pope said unaffordable dental costs had led to people “raiding their future retirement savings … or simply deferring the economic pain of a trip to the dentist while putting up with the inevitable physical pain.”

Walk-in basis

Under the proposal, seven of the public dental clinics would be located in Melbourne and three in regional Victoria, in areas where there are gaps in services.

The clinics would be open from 9am to 9pm on weekdays and 9am to 5pm on weekends and would operate on a walk-in basis, with priority given to people with the most urgent needs, including those experiencing dental pain or swelling or who have had an accident.

Asked on Saturday if the clinics would means test arrivals, Carroll said “we will be focusing on those people that don’t have private health insurance that need the care that they need”.

Once fully operational, the government said they would treat more than 100,000 Victorians a year.

The state’s urgent care clinics were similarly unveiled just three months before the 2022 Victorian election as part of a joint announcement with New South Wales.

On Saturday, a spokesperson for the NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said the government “would like to see more detail on the Victorian model but it’s not something we’re actively considering right now”.

The federal government also began contributing funding to the clinics and expanded the rollout.

Asked on Saturday if the Victorian government would seek federal funding, Carroll said: “No, this is a statewide initiative.”

Dental costing Australians big

Across most of Australia, free or low-cost dental care is currently only available to specific eligible groups such as children and young people, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and those with concession cards.

In Victoria, $239m was allocated in the 2026-27 budget to dental, including the Smile Squad program in public schools.

But Medicare does not cover dental care for most adults, leaving millions of Australians to choose between dipping into their wallets or skipping treatment.

According to Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) data, Australia spends more than $12bn on dental services. About 61% of that cost falls to the individual, health insurance funds cover 19%, and the federal government 11% and state governments 8%. There has also been a sharp rise in applications to access superannuation early to fund dental treatment.

Guardian Australia reported in 2025 that people struggling to afford dental bills were delaying or skipping treatment, while untreated tooth decay was increasing and record numbers of Australians were presenting to hospitals for dental procedures.

Later that year, during the federal election, the Greens campaigned heavily on their plan to expand Medicare to cover dental services for adults, which was costed at $195bn over 10 years. The party went backwards at the election but continues to pursue the policy.

Federal Labor backbenchers have also previously expressed support for putting dental treatment into Medicare and it remains in the party platform.

In Victoria, Labor sources are hopeful Carroll’s announcement will shift the party into campaign mode after weeks spent seeking to differentiate himself from his predecessors, Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, including by calling a royal commission into the construction sector and pausing the passage of work from home legislation.

However, sources have said the dental policy was developed under Allan and her team.

australia.title: Sorrow as community pays tribute to ‘shining light’ Lily Hooper after NSW hiking tragedy
australia.snippet: The 18-year-old remembered as a talented athlete with an infectious smile and ‘one of those people who everyone simply liked’ Get our bre...
australia.content:
Tributes have flowed for 18-year-old Lily Hooper, remembered as an adventurous, multitalented athlete with an infectious smile, after her body was found on Thursday afternoon, eight days after she disappeared while hiking in the New South Wales southern highlands.

The teenager was a fixture across local sporting and community groups in the Wollondilly region, training in martial arts, alongside her job as a Sydney BridgeClimb guide.

In her home town of Oakdale, the community gathered for a vigil on Friday evening at Willis park. By Saturday morning, the park fence was adorned with flowers, fairy lights and electric candles.

The Wollondilly Performing Arts Centre and the shire library were illuminated in purple. The mayor, Matt Gould, said on Friday that the community had rarely been as devastated.

“From 5pm this afternoon and across the weekend, Willis Park at Oakdale will become a place for our community to come together and remember Lily Hooper,” Gould said, adding that Red Cross volunteers were on site “to support anyone who may need someone to talk to”.

“[It’s] just an opportunity for everyone to come together and show the level of support there is for the family, and just to look out for each other.”

Flags across the region, including at the Oakdale Rural Fire Service, flew at half mast. The brigade said in a statement that the community is navigating a “deep sorrow … as we all remember the shining light that has touched so many of us”.

‘A talented and tough martial artist’

Hooper trained at Toodokan Self Defence Academy, which cancelled classes on Thursday afternoon after the news. The academy said in a tribute that Lily was “a beautiful soul, taken far too soon”.

Her martial arts instructor, Mark Szalajko, said he would miss her smile and conversation, describing her as a talented, tough fighter.

“She was a talented and tough martial artist, but despite that toughness, Lily was such a lovely person. She was one of those people who everyone simply liked,” he said. “I will really miss her smile, her conversations and the moments we shared on the mat.”

Further tributes came from the Oaks Netball Club, which said it was “devastated by the loss”, with members to wear black armbands in her memory at games over the weekend.

The Burragorang District Soccer Club also posted a tribute on social media in Hooper’s honour: “Our community has lost a truly beautiful person, and our hearts are heavy with sadness.”

Hooper’s high school, Campbelltown Performing Arts – where she graduated in 2025 – remembered her as a “kind, humorous and respectful young woman who lit up every room with her infectious smile, positive energy and determination to live life to its fullest”.

“I am so proud of the woman you became … You are so loved my musical angel,” one commenter wrote under the school’s tribute.

Another commented “I feel incredibly privileged to have known her and to have shared so many memorable moments with her. What I will remember most is the loyalty she had for her beautiful best friends.”

Sydney Harbour BridgeClimb, where Hooper worked as a guide, issued a statement saying she was “an absolute delight from the moment she joined and lit up every space with her smile and enthusiasm”.

“She was compassionate, a friend to all, motivated and had a positive impact on everyone she connected with,” a spokesperson said. “Her loss is felt deeply throughout our team, and Lily’s family and loved ones are in our thoughts and our hearts, today and always.”

Police initially told Hooper’s family she was alive, with footage circulated by Channel Seven showing the elation of friends and family. Her father, Jim Hooper, showed off a guitar and packet of Tim Tams he had brought to the site “because it might lure her out of the bush”. Hope was shattered barely 30 minutes later.

The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, later told reporters in Goulburn that the devastating miscommunication was “born out of elation”.

“Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously, we know now, an impact on her family,” Lanyon said.

The assistant commissioner Joseph Cassar told reporters in Moss Vale on Thursday afternoon that the searchers had carried handheld radios and faced communication challenges in the “thick, dense terrain”.

Hooper, an experienced hiker, had been found dead off the trail, a “significant distance” from her car.

The Wollondilly Rotary Club established a fundraiser to support the Hooper family after her disappearance.

“Lily’s kindness, spirit, and connection to the Oakdale and Wollondilly regions, along with her family, has touched many lives, and our club is committed to standing beside her family during this difficult time,” the club said in a statement.

australia.title: Coles website down after viral Reddit post sees customers buy cases of alcoholic drinks at nearly 80% discount
australia.snippet: Supermarket’s website and app go offline as customers save more than $100 on some 24-packs Get our breaking news email , free app or dail...
australia.content:
The Coles website and app have gone offline hours after a viral Reddit post highlighted a nearly 80% discount on 24-packs of premixed alcoholic drinks.

For several hours on Saturday, both the Coles website and app displayed a message advising “we’re currently offline – but not for long”. The website and app came back online, before the website went down again during the afternoon. It was back up at about 4pm AEST.

It came after a post by an Australian Reddit account on Friday about a discount on 24-packs of Jack Daniel’s & Cola 330ml bottles sold via Coles by subsidiary Liquorland which were marked down from $130 to $27, a saving of $103, or just under 80%.

“Found this. I’m assuming it’s a mistake?!” wrote the account, which is run by the operators of price tracking website CW Scanner.

They subsequently noticed similar discounts, lowering the price of 24-packs of premixed drinks and beer to a price similar to that of discounted four- or six-packs.

The operators of CW Scanner told Guardian Australia that the post had received more than 180,000 views. Other users described ordering online with the discounts, which did not appear on the Liquorland website itself, with one having it matched at their local liquor store.

But on Saturday, Reddit users noticed the Coles website had gone down, while some later wrote that their orders had been cancelled by Coles. The Coles website and app came back online briefly on Saturday afternoon, with the beer and premixed drinks categories removed. The website subsequently went offline again.

In a statement on Saturday afternoon, a Coles spokesperson said it was aware of a technical issue affecting its website and app, and “was working quickly to restore services”.

“Due to a technical error, select 24-pack beer and RTD [ready-to-drink] products were incorrectly priced on our website,” they said.

“The error has been corrected, and impacted customers are being notified. Any customers charged for the affected items will be refunded in accordance with our normal refund process. We apologise for the error and any inconvenience caused.”

CW Scanner identified at least 20 24-packs – or cartons – of beer and 46 cases of premixed drinks affected by the discounts, with the average discount on beer about $49, and premixed drinks $111.

The largest discount, on 24-packs of Smirnoff Crush Mango & Peach Zero Sugar 6% 440ml cans, provided a saving of $173, down to $29 from $202.

Using data from CW Scanner, the Guardian has reported that promotional prices switched on and off at Coles and Woolworths largely in sync over the past two years.

Earlier this year, a court found Coles’ “Down Down” promotions in some cases falsely led customers to believe they were enjoying a true price reduction.

australia.title: Northern Territory’s Karlu Karlu conservation reserve recognised as a rare International Dark Sky Sanctuary
australia.snippet: Sacred site joins 23 other sites worldwide known for their exceptionally clear night sky, free from light pollution, after submission fro...
australia.content:
A remote natural landmark in the Northern Territory has been officially crowned an International Dark Sky Sanctuary, making it the Territory’s first and only the third in Australia.

Karlu Karlu conservation reserve, also known as the Devils Marbles, is located about 100km south of Tennant Creek and is known for its ancient granite boulders.

Almost all of the reserve’s 1,800 hectares is a sacred site, significant to the Kaytetye, Warumungu, Warlpiri and Alyawarra traditional owners.

International Dark Sky Sanctuaries are places recognised for their exceptionally clear night skies and protected natural environments. The sites are typically in remote areas with little light pollution and are valued for their scientific, environmental, educational or cultural significance.

The designation is difficult to achieve, with only 24 recognised locations worldwide.

Arkaroola Wilderness Sanctuary, located in the Flinders Ranges in South Australia, and the Australian Age of Dinosaurs Museum of Natural History, which sits atop the Jump-Up mesa in Queensland, are the only other designated locations in Australia, achieving that status in 2023 and 2019 respectively.

The NT designation follows a submission led by the Department of Tourism and Hospitality, with support from the traditional owners and local councils.

Being granted the designation involved “an extensive year-long process” led by NT Parks and Wildlife. It includes six months of night-sky readings to measure darkness levels, a review of artificial lighting and an assessment of future risks to preserving the night sky.

Philip Cowan, the senior director of NT Parks and Wildlife Operations, told Guardian Australia that the designation represents “a commitment to protect and promote the night sky”.

Light pollution will need to be considered in any future development, he said.

“Karlu Karlu has some of the darkest skies in the world,” Cowan said. “You can view the Milky Way and the constellations free from any light pollution, and we are excited to share them with our visitors.”

Cowan said keeping the night sky free from light pollution “helps our native animals and is also good for human health”.

Tourism and Events NT’s CEO, Suzana Bishop, called the outcome “fantastic news both for the visitor economy and future conservation of this special place”.

“The international recognition puts the region on the map, adding to our offerings for visitors seeking unobscured star-filled skies and experiences,” she said.

australia.title: Home comforts: can remote work be better for the environment?
australia.snippet: Many Australians now have the option to work from home. But is it better or worse for the environment? Change by degrees offers life hack...
australia.content:
The normalisation of working from home and flexible work has been one of the Covid-19 pandemic’s few positive legacies.

Today more than a third of Australians – and most managers and professionals – spend at least some of their working lives out of the office, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

In Victoria, the former premier Jacinta Allan proposed giving workers the right to work from home at least two days a week. But after business pushback and with a November election on the horizon, the incoming premier, Ben Carroll, delayed the start from September to July next year.

Of course, not everyone has the opportunity to work from home. Digital access varies, few homes have room for an office, and many jobs – including retail, trades and hospitality, and health and aged care professions – require employees to be in-person or on-site.

But for those who can, there’s broad agreement that working from home can be positive for the environment, although the extent of the benefits varies, depending on employee and business behaviours.

What are the environmental benefits?

A well-publicised US study found people choosing to work from home full-time could reduce their emissions by up to 54%. But those savings may be curbed by the fact that remote workers are more likely to increase their emissions for social and recreational activities, such as using the car to run errands.

An Australian study suggests that emission cuts from transport changes outweigh residential energy use increases, concluding that if employees in capital cities worked from home 1.5 to four days a week this might reduce national emissions by 1.2m to 5.8m tonnes.

A 2026 International Energy Agency report recommends working from home to displace oil use from commuting, with the agency’s figures noting that everyone working remotely one day a week could save 24m tonnes of CO2 annually.

Alan Pears, an expert in energy efficiency and a senior industry fellow at RMIT, says there will always be huge variation in environmental savings, depending on people’s remote work behaviours, distance from work and transport mode.

For example, emissions savings from staying at home may be limited for people who usually travel to work by foot, bike or public transport, but more significant for those with long car commutes. In most cases, home energy use – from running computers, lighting, heating or cooling – is likely to rise, although any resulting emissions may be limited for homes with solar, or on renewable energy plans. Careful choices can increase the benefits.

“It’s not just the immediate emissions reductions,” Pears says. “Receiving a big energy bill could motivate energy saving investments in the home that benefit beyond work. Avoiding travel time can be a very valuable benefit including flexibility for family duties, avoiding childcare costs … It may mean the household can run one less car.”

Does working from home reduce car travel and congestion?

Working from home is a good policy for cities and regions struggling with car pollution and congestion as it can have measurable impacts on reducing traffic-related pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions, says Dorina Pojani, associate professor in urban planning at the University of Queensland.

Australian cities’ transport systems are largely designed around work-based commutes, and those working from home will avoid the need to drive at peak times. “People might still travel, but just travel at different times in the day,” Pojani says.

“People with cars might end up running errands so the overall amount of travel might not change, or be even greater. One of the knock-on effects is that people start moving to more affordable, outer suburban or regional locations and their commute, when they do visit the office, would become even longer.” Without careful planning, an unintended consequence may be increased car travel on in-office days, and lower overall public transport access and use.

While energy use and workplace comfort used to be a primary concern of employers, the work from home trend has left more employees footing the bill for energy use and comfort.

Research from the University of Sydney’s school of architecture, design and planning has measured the effect of the home work environments on both comfort and productivity, but also residential energy usage.

Associate Prof Jungsoo Kim, an author of the research, says the effect of working from home on household energy usage varies greatly according to many factors. But using simulation data from homes in Sydney, the research found that the overall increase in annual household energy use and emissions was more modest than has been often assumed.

“If someone converts a previously unused room into a dedicated home office and heats or cools that space throughout the day, household energy use can increase noticeably. In contrast, if work takes place in a space that would already be occupied, such as a living room, the additional energy demand is relatively small.”

If you can work from home, here’s how to maximise the benefits

The environmental benefits of remote work are highly dependent on how workers and employers navigate the logistics of their working lives.

Pojani says one of the most effective things people can do to maximise the environmental benefits is using low or zero emissions transport such as walking, biking or e-biking or public transport to run local errands and school or childcare drop-offs and pick-ups, instead of “reaching for the car keys”.

She also recommends embracing shared work environments, especially for those without the space for a home office. “There are now many neighbourhood co-working spaces, and businesses should look at subsidising monthly membership for such arrangements so they no longer need to pay to rent as much office space in the city.”

There are other social and economic factors to consider. According to the ABS, people who choose to work from home cite many reasons, including more flexible hours, the ability to catch up on work, less time commuting and family responsibilities.

Pojani says she fully supports Australian states legislating to make working from home a legal right for workers. “It’s absolutely a positive for society and the environment. We can’t separate these things. We need to strike a sort of win-win balance where both the environment and society benefit.”

world.title: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal
world.snippet: Agreement is among largest third-country deportations driven by Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Twenty deportees from the Un...
world.content:
Twenty deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement that will see the west African country receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The group arrived at the Roberts international airport outside the capital, Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements pursued by the administration since Trump returned to office last year.

The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberia’s justice minister, Natu Oswald Tweh, said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the west African country if they wished.

The US has agreed to extend visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months and pledged $124m in assistance as part of the arrangement.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that are not their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa. A new report by Refugees International and Human Rights First say the Trump administration has reached deals with at least 35 countries and has sent roughly 23,000 people to 26 of them as of early August, and makes the Liberia agreement the largest single arrangement so far.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

A February report by Senate foreign relations committee Democrats found the Trump administration had paid more than $32m to five governments, several with poor human rights records, to accept about 300 third-country deportees – including $1.1m per person to Rwanda for seven deportees, and $7.5m to Equatorial Guinea for 29, a sum exceeding all US aid to that country over the previous eight years.

The report found more than 80% of those sent to third countries had since returned home anyway, often at further cost to taxpayers, and cited cases where deportees with US court-ordered protections were removed to Ghana and Equatorial Guinea before being sent onward within days.

The state department disputed the report’s characterization of its enforcement record.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic
world.snippet: The collapse was caused by a landslide, while local officials say the death toll is likely to rise as recovery efforts continue More than...
world.content:
More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday.

The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon. Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them.

A statement by a local public prosecutor said many others were trapped under the deluge. It did not mention the number of fatalities. However, Gervais Ganagoroh, a Red Cross volunteer involved in the relief effort, told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that more than 100 bodies had been recovered from the collapse and ⁠a senior official at a local mining association confirmed that number to Reuters.

Local media in CAR reported that authorities had launched an investigation into the incident. A second prosecutor from Baboua told the press that the incident is believed to have been caused by “the collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating”.

“The ground completely collapsed and buried people,” Cedric Mbango, a miner at the site, told the AFP news agency, describing the incident as “catastrophic”.

Rescuers are racing to retrieve the bodies of victims and find survivors among the miners, believed to be nationals of CAR and Cameroon. Authorities in Cameroon’s Eastern region said at least three of its citizens have been identified as victims in the incident.

Grégoire Mvongo, the region’s governor told state-owned radio on Wednesday that he was “working in close collaboration with our Central African colleagues to deal with the aftermath of this tragedy”.

Bertrand Be Yangué, a member of the Zamboye youth council, said that “finding them alive would be a miracle.” He added: “We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair.”

The toll is expected to rise as the rescue efforts continue, added Yangué.

The Central African news website Corbeau News reported that heavy machinery, including tractors, was being used in the retrieval mission and could jeopardise the rescue of those still alive under the landmass.

The exact number of people who were in the mine at the time of the cave-in remains unknown.

Small scale artisanal mines are common in different parts of Africa, despite regulations criminalising them, as unemployment continues to drive able-bodied men to abandoned or unused mines, to eke a living. The mining sites often operate with weak safety standards leading to repeated incidents: at least 40 people have died in several mining incidents in CAR this year alone.

world.title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya
world.snippet: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief Seven people, including five ...
world.content:
Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.

Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.

Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.

In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”

The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.

“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.

The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.

Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.

Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.

The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.

Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.

In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”

Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.

Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.

In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

world.title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn
world.snippet: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back Europe live – latest u...
world.content:
The Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.

The majority of the estimated 70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta – a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.

On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain and Morocco work together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”

The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.

To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.

Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.

News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.

The People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.

The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.

According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of last March 21,104 people aged 16-23 were under guardianship of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo now deadliest in country’s history
world.snippet: At least 2,325 people have died from the virus, according to official data, with outbreak on track to be biggest in history The Ebola out...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history, with at least 2,325 people dead, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak.

The DRC’s public health institute said confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest in history. The 2014-16 outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.

On Friday, the UN said Ebola “is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo” and said the epidemic was killing one person every 30 minutes.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have made this outbreak – the 17th in the country’s history – the fastest-growing in the known history of the virus. It took almost five months for the 2014-16 west Africa outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths, compared with more than 2,000 deaths in less than three months in this outbreak.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments yet for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current surge in cases. Nonetheless, 1,000 people in the DRC have recovered from the infection, with 730 still in healthcare or isolation facilities.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the strain began last month in Ituri. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said last week that two vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo were now being tested on people.

Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to the DRC with Médecins Sans Frontières, said: “Normally, as an outbreak progresses, the case fatality ratio should fall as contact tracing improves and patients are identified and treated earlier. Instead, we’re still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community.”

Uganda has reported at least 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case reported there was on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

In May, the WHO declared the outbreak in the DRC and Uganda as a public health emergency of international concern. It said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier, in February.

Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to the WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

The response to this outbreak has been hampered by attacks on healthcare facilities, often fuelled by misinformation about safe burial practices, as well as strikes by some unpaid health workers. Decades of unrest and outside interference on traumatised communities, as well as poor health and road infrastructure have also complicated the picture.

More than 70% of people die in the community and not in health centres, said Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional Africa director.

Jean-Paul Malo Lotsima, a civil society official in the Djugu area of Ituri, told the AFP news agency: “People prefer to be treated at home, thinking it is a case of poisoning or some other illness.”

He added: “It’s often at the last minute, when the family realises that the situation is getting worse, that patients are taken to hospital. And sometimes, they die on the way.”

Flavier Ngurima, who lives in Nizi, one of the hotspots of the outbreak in Ituri, said his brother died before reaching the treatment centre. “We had called on a nurse from the family to treat him at home because the patient and the family members were afraid to go to the ETC [treatment centre],” he said. “They said that over there, a lot of people die.”
